title: Wojciech Zaremba - Building Resilience for the Intelligence Age

segments.text: WOJCIECH ZAREMBA: Wonderful.
Thank you guys for having me here.
OK.
Slides.
So as it was mentioned, I'm part of OpenAI Foundation.
This is an interesting entity.
OpenAI went through restructured a number of months ago,
and now, there is a nonprofit that
owns around one quarter of OpenAI equity.
So that's like a massive amount of resources.
And one of the divisions of OpenAI Foundation
is AI resilience.
I'm going to explain today what AI resilience is.
And it's similar to AI safety, and yet it's different.
So today, I will explain what AI resilience is.
And I found it to be the most useful to explain it
through analogy to fire resilience.
And then we'll go into what does it mean for AI playing out well.
So how the presentation will go will
be at first, describing similarities
between fire and AI.
And obviously, fire is very different than I
in many, many ways.
So these are by no means perfect.
So both fire and AI are general purpose technologies.
It means that they have really broad applicability.
In case of fire, it was used or it
is used to heat food, provide warmth to people, smelter metal.
It's part of engines.
It's pretty much fundamental to our civilization.
Something similar is happening with AI.
AI is now part of the knowledge and wisdom development,
part of the scientific process.
And also if you take seriously where robotics is going,
it will be just the fundamental part of the economic engine
of the future.
So both AI and fire are general purpose technologies.
That's one similarity.
Another similarity is both technologies come with risks.
So in case of fire, there's a number
of major fires in the past.
London was burned four times, Boston, Chicago.
Like 80% of London was consumed during the large fires.
And now today, we pretty well understand
the risks coming from fire.
That's less true about AI.
When you ask people about the risks of AI,
it's kind of like a people point in different directions.
There are like many things pointed out.
It's just enough to open a newspaper
and hear what people are scared about.
And I would say, these risks are highly uncertain.
It actually might turn out that some of these risks will end up
being a vaporware, and some of them will turn out to be 10x
more than what people expected, and some of the risks might not
even be at the least.
So fire and AI, they come with risks.
Here is an interesting twist in the story.
So it turns out that in case of fire,
the way how people try to provide a safety for fire
was through restriction.
So curfew comes from French, and it means extinguish fire.
In the medieval time, it was common
that if you had fire going on at your home during the night,
police would come and knock at your door
and ask it to extinguish fire.
So obviously, that's like a decrease
of capabilities of the fire.
And it also turned out that at least in this particular case,
actually, it didn't work out well.
The Great Fire of London happened despite of curfews.
So the method of restricting fire
didn't actually work out for this particular technology.
Now, in case of AI restrictions, this is a more complicated.
There are some restrictions that actually
seem to be working pretty well.
An example would be most of the platforms,
they follow non-consensual intimate images restriction.
They don't allow for this.
Now, some people advocated for open source restrictions,
and these are not really implemented.
So I would say that in case of AI,
the restrictions didn't work out well.
So now, you might ask actually what
did it take for a fire to become safe?
And it turns out that there wasn't a silver bullet.
It's not that there is a single solution to make fire safe.
And it ends up being multi-layered ecosystem
approach.
So you have these systems for early detection of a fire.
There are also people who are trained toward dealing
with fire, brigades.
They have a special vehicles.
There are fire trucks.
They have a specially designed hoses.
Now, it turns out that the cities, they
have a supply of water spread throughout the city with fire
hydrants at the sufficient pressure
and the quantity necessary in order to extinguish fire.
There are also materials, which are specially designed.
So we switch from wood to metal and concrete.
There are also inspections, insurance, and also
let's say, designated areas for exit and so on and so forth.
So once we implemented this, actually, now, fire
is not something that we are particularly worried about.
So we are in the place that none of us
is worried about this particular risks.
We are able to really fully harness the benefits.
So you might ask, actually, did it even work?
And the claim is it actually worked remarkably well.
So these days, we have cities which
are order of magnitude denser than the medieval cities.
We have many more sources of fire,
so there's a let's say, electricity, gas industry,
and even data centers these days.
And fire is not something that people are worried about.
So now you might ask, OK, what would it
be analogous for the AI itself?
And I find that people in AI space,
they try to think about the silver bullet.
That there would be one solution in order for AI
to play out well.
And I actually think that that's an incorrect way
of thinking about it.
I also think that it's not just enough to make
an individual models aligned, though that's
like a part of the solution.
There needs to be a number of solutions in the ecosystem.
So what I mean by that.
Let me give you some examples.
In case of the models become, for instance,
quite capable when it comes to biological domain.
And many people foresee the risks
coming from models, making it easy to manufacture pandemics.
Now, if we think that that's the risk,
then dealing with these risks requires--
and if we also assume that there will be diffusion
of advanced open source models, then it
might not be sufficient to guardrail these capabilities
within the frontier labs.
That's one of the things that should be done,
but that won't be enough.
We might need to harden the environment itself.
So, for instance, in that space, people
are thinking about ideas like sanitizing air.
Because if air is sanitized, then actually pathogens
wouldn't be able to spread.
Maybe in case of cybersecurity, we need to get to that point
that the software is formally verified.
That would prevent it from being hacked by superintelligence.
Maybe in case of safety accidents,
we need the public database similar to how
it's happening in case of aviation
that the incidents are being publicly reported
and the ones who reported gained by reporting a safe harbor
and so on and so forth.
So now, creation of this might--
some of them could be achieved through creation
of the companies working on these efforts.
Some of them might be achieved through the creation
of the nonprofits.
But fundamentally, we are in the place
that it would be important for a number of capable people,
for people who are like a reality warping,
for people's CEO like figures to ask themselves
what needs to be built in the world for the AI
to play out well, and then to go after building
the new institutions and organizations.
And in case of OpenAI Foundation,
we have tons of resources to support endeavors like that.
And whether or not AI resilience will succeed
depends on people in this room.
Thank you guys very much.
[APPLAUSE]
